claim: Approximately one-third of the proteome in animals is localized at the various membranes of the cell.
source: In animals, approximately one-third of the proteome is localized at the various membranes of the cell, while more than 50% of the currently available pharmaceuticals target membrane proteins (Santos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2017

claim: More than 50% of currently available pharmaceuticals target membrane proteins.
source: In animals, approximately one-third of the proteome is localized at the various membranes of the cell, while more than 50% of the currently available pharmaceuticals target membrane proteins (Santos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2017

claim: Single-molecule FRET has a limited dynamic range covering less than 10 nm.
source: However, with its limited dynamic range covering <10 nm as well as the need to introduce both donor and acceptor dyes with high fidelity and efficiency often obstructs its application.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about FRET limitations

claim: Single-molecule localization microscopy is limited by axial localization precision of approximately 10 nm.
source: Single-molecule localization microscopy in turn is limited by axial localization precision of ~10 nm (Gwosch et al., 2020; Schmidt et al., 2008; Shtengel et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gwosch et al., 2020; Schmidt et al., 2008; Shtengel et al., 2009

claim: Graphene has an atomic thickness that ensures high optical transparency.
source: The atomic thickness of graphene ensures high optical transparency and an extremely high confinement of plasmons (106 times the diffraction limit) (Koppens et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koppens et al., 2011

claim: Graphene provides an extremely high confinement of plasmons (10^6 times the diffraction limit).
source: The atomic thickness of graphene ensures high optical transparency and an extremely high confinement of plasmons (106 times the diffraction limit) (Koppens et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koppens et al., 2011

claim: Metal-induced energy transfer (MIET) has a dynamic range that extends over a distance of approximately 150 nm.
source: Compared to metal-induced energy transfer (MIET) (Chizhik et al., 2014), with a dynamic range that extends over a distance of ~150 nm, graphene-induced energy transfer (GIET) occurs within a dynamic range of ~30 nm, thus covering the dimensions of large membrane protein complexes (Ghosh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chizhik et al., 2014

claim: Graphene-induced energy transfer (GIET) occurs within a dynamic range of approximately 30 nm.
source: Compared to metal-induced energy transfer (MIET) (Chizhik et al., 2014), with a dynamic range that extends over a distance of ~150 nm, graphene-induced energy transfer (GIET) occurs within a dynamic range of ~30 nm, thus covering the dimensions of large membrane protein complexes (Ghosh et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ghosh et al., 2019

claim: A mass signal of lipid deposition on graphene of 2.5 ng/mm² was observed after washing out excess vesicles.
source: A mass signal of lipid deposition on graphene of 2.5 ng/mm² was observed after washing out excess vesicles (Figure 1B).
evidence: Measured by TIRFS-RIF detection as shown in Figure 1B

claim: For trisNTA-functionalized lipid bilayer formation by vesicle fusion on a silica surface, a lipid deposition of 5 ng/mm² was observed.
source: For trisNTA-functionalized lipid bilayer formation by vesicle fusion on a silica surface, which has been previously established for protein interaction analysis at membranes (Beutel et al., 2014; Gavutis et al., 2005; Lata et al., 2006), a lipid deposition of 5 ng/mm² was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Measured by TIRFS-RIF detection as shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The lipid deposition measurements confirmed formation of a lipid monolayer on the hydrophobic graphene surface.
source: These results confirmed formation of a lipid monolayer on the hydrophobic graphene surface.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of lipid deposition on graphene (2.5 ng/mm²) versus silica (5 ng/mm²)

claim: GIET efficiency for mEGFP bound to NB-H6 on graphene was 83.6%.
source: Comparing the mEGFP fluorescence signal observed on graphene (IG) to that on the silica substrate (I0) confirmed strong quenching by GIET with an efficiency of 83.6% for mEGFP bound to NB-H6.
evidence: Calculated from fluorescence intensity measurements on graphene versus silica

claim: Direct immobilization of H6-tagged mEGFP on graphene resulted in GIET efficiency of 92.4%.
source: Direct immobilization of H6-tagged mEGFP on graphene resulted into even stronger GIET (Figure 1D) with an efficiency of 92.4%.
evidence: Calculated from fluorescence intensity measurements shown in Figure 1D

claim: The size of the anti-GFP nanobody is approximately 2 nm based on the crystal structure.
source: As the size of NB is ~2 nm based on the crystal structure (Kirchhofer et al., 2010), these results highlight that GIET can reveal nanoscale distances of proteins immobilized on a graphene-supported lipid monolayer.
evidence: Based on crystal structure from Kirchhofer et al., 2010

claim: GIET can reveal nanoscale distances of proteins immobilized on a graphene-supported lipid monolayer.
source: As the size of NB is ~2 nm based on the crystal structure (Kirchhofer et al., 2010), these results highlight that GIET can reveal nanoscale distances of proteins immobilized on a graphene-supported lipid monolayer.
evidence: Inferred from the ability to detect the ~2 nm difference between direct and NB-mediated mEGFP binding

claim: DNA nanorulers with 20mer, 25mer, 35mer, and 50mer nucleotides were designed as scaffolds for calibration.
source: Four single strand DNA (ssDNA) with 20mer, 25mer, 35mer, and 50mer nucleotides were designed as the scaffold of nanorulers (Figure 2A, DNA sequences in Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: Experimental design described in text and shown in Figure 2A

claim: The DNA nanorulers share a common 20mer sequence at the 5´-end and cholesterol modification at the 3´-end for anchoring into the lipid monolayer.
source: These ssDNAs share a common 20mer sequence at the 5´-end and cholesterol modification at the 3´-end for anchoring into the lipid monolayer (Johnson-Buck et al., 2014) (anchor strand).
evidence: Design based on approach from Johnson-Buck et al., 2014

claim: 5% negatively charged DOPS was incorporated into the DOPC matrix to promote perpendicular orientation of oligonucleotides by electrostatic repulsion.
source: To promote, by electrostatic repulsion, perpendicular orientation of oligonucleotides with respect to lipid layer, 5% negatively charged 1,2-di-(9Z-octadecenoyl)-sn-glycero-3-phospho-L-serine (DOPS) was incorporated into the DOPC matrix.
evidence: Experimental design to control DNA orientation

claim: The obtained correlation of IG/I0 vs d matches the predicted GIET curve well with a globally fitted tilting angle of (43 ± 1)°.
source: Strikingly, the obtained correlation of IG/I0 vs d matches the predicted GIET curve well with a globally fitted tilting angle of (43 ± 1)° (Figure 2B), confirming the distance-dependent GIET on graphene-supported lipid monolayer.
evidence: Obtained from fitting experimental data to theoretical model as shown in Figure 2B

claim: GIET has a dynamic range within 3–25 nm corresponding to changes in GIET efficiency from 93–15%.
source: Results of both intensity and lifetime measurements showed a dynamic range within 3–25 nm corresponding to changes in GIET efficiency from 93–15%.
evidence: Determined from DNA nanoruler calibration experiments

claim: A significant difference was detected for nanorulers between 35–5´F and 35–3´F, confirming that GIET is robust for detecting distance changes of approximately 1.2 nm between 6 nm and 11 nm.
source: A significant difference was detected for nanorulers between 35–5´F and 35–3´F, confirming that GIET is robust for detecting distance changes of ~1.2 nm between 6 nm and 11 nm.
evidence: Demonstrated by comparing two DNA nanoruler configurations

claim: Ratios of fluorescence lifetimes on graphene (τG) to those on glass (τ0) closely matched the corresponding intensity ratios.
source: Ratios of fluorescence lifetimes on graphene (τG) to those on glass (τ0) closely matched the corresponding intensity ratios, which further corroborated the simulated distance-dependent GIET efficiency (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: Comparison of lifetime and intensity measurements shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 1C

claim: For H6-mEGFP directly tethered to the membrane, the axial distance was estimated to be 1.3 nm.
source: For the axial organization of mEGFP and mEGFP:NB complex tethered to the DOPC monolayer surface via trisNTA-DODA, distances 1.3 nm for H6-mEGFP directly tethered to the membrane (IG/I0: 7.6%) and 3.0 nm for mEGFP captured via NB-H6 (IG/I0: 16.4%) were estimated.
evidence: Calculated from GIET efficiency measurements using calibration curve

claim: For mEGFP captured via NB-H6, the axial distance was estimated to be 3.0 nm.
source: For the axial organization of mEGFP and mEGFP:NB complex tethered to the DOPC monolayer surface via trisNTA-DODA, distances 1.3 nm for H6-mEGFP directly tethered to the membrane (IG/I0: 7.6%) and 3.0 nm for mEGFP captured via NB-H6 (IG/I0: 16.4%) were estimated.
evidence: Calculated from GIET efficiency measurements using calibration curve

claim: The distance of 1.7 nm induced by the nanobody is in good agreement with the crystal structure of the GFP-NB complex.
source: The distance of 1.7 nm induced by the nanobody is in good agreement with the crystal structure of the GFP-NB complex (Kirchhofer et al., 2010), highlighting the nanometer sensitivity of quantifying the axial position of proteins onto lipid monolayers by GIET.
evidence: Comparison with crystal structure from Kirchhofer et al., 2010

claim: Upon hybridizing the 35mer anchor strand with the 20mer 3´ FAM probe strand, a fluorescence lifetime τG of 0.24 ± 0.02 ns was detected.
source: Upon hybridizing with the 20mer 3´ FAM probe strand, a fluorescence lifetime τG of 0.24 ± 0.02 ns was detected (Figure 2D).
evidence: Measured by TCSPC as shown in Figure 2D

claim: The τG/τ0 ratio of 8.0 ± 0.6% for the 35mer anchor strand with 20mer probe corresponds to a distance of 4.4 ± 0.2 nm from the graphene.
source: Comparing to τ0 of 3.04 ns on glass, the obtained τG/τ0 ratio of 8.0 ± 0.6% corresponds to a distance of 4.4 ± 0.2 nm from the graphene (1.9 nm from the lipid headgroups), suggesting that the hybridized probe-anchor DNA strand collapses onto the surface of the lipid monolayer due to the flexible, unpaired 15mer gap.
evidence: Calculated from lifetime measurements using calibration curve

claim: Addition of a 15mer ssDNA blocker strand resulted in approximately sixfold increase of the fluorescence lifetime to 1.50 ± 0.03 ns.
source: To test the hypothesis, a 15mer ssDNA blocker strand was added, resulting into a ~ sixfold increase of the fluorescence lifetime (1.50 ± 0.03 ns, Figure 2D).
evidence: Measured by TCSPC as shown in Figure 2D

claim: The τG/τ0 ratio of 49 ± 1.0% after adding the blocker corresponds to a distance of 10.9 ± 0.2 nm.
source: The τG/τ0 ratio of 49 ± 1.0% corresponds to a distance of 10.9 ± 0.2 nm, that is a height of 8.4 nm above the lipid layer.
evidence: Calculated from lifetime measurements using calibration curve

claim: The height of 8.4 nm above the lipid layer corresponds to a tilting angle α = 45° for the 35mer DNA nanoruler.
source: Compared to the length of the 35mer DNA nanoruler (11.9 nm), the height corresponds to a tilting angle α = 45°, which is in good agreement with the tilting angle α obtained for the calibration.
evidence: Calculated from geometric relationship between measured height and DNA length

claim: Lateral diffusion dynamics of anchored DNA strands were not observed in FRAP experiments.
source: However, we did not observe lateral diffusion dynamics of anchored DNA strands as explored by fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP, Figure 2—figure supplement 5), thus ensuring that changes in fluorescence lifetime are not related to changes in the lateral organization within the lipid monolayer.
evidence: Demonstrated by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5

claim: Ypt7 is a Rab7-like GTPase that functions as a functional marker of the late endosomal membrane.
source: This process is initiated by the Rab7-like GTPase Ypt7 as a functional marker of the late endosomal membrane (Figure 3A).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of Ypt7 function

claim: Mon1-Ccz1 is the guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) for Ypt7 on endosomes and vacuoles.
source: Upon activation by its guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Mon1-Ccz1 on endosomes and vacuoles (Nordmann et al., 2010), Ypt7-GTP recruits the 650 kDa heterohexameric HOPS tethering complex (Brett et al., 2008; Ostrowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nordmann et al., 2010

claim: The HOPS tethering complex is a 650 kDa heterohexameric complex.
source: Upon activation by its guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) Mon1-Ccz1 on endosomes and vacuoles (Nordmann et al., 2010), Ypt7-GTP recruits the 650 kDa heterohexameric HOPS tethering complex (Brett et al., 2008; Ostrowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brett et al., 2008; Ostrowicz et al., 2010

claim: HOPS has four central subunits: Vps11, Vps18, Vps16, and Vps33.
source: HOPS has four central subunits Vps11, Vps18, Vps16, and Vps33 (Rieder and Emr, 1997), which are flanked by Vps39 and Vps41 as Rab-specific subunits at its tail and head, respectively (Brett et al., 2008; Bröcker et al., 2012; Ostrowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rieder and Emr, 1997

claim: Vps39 and Vps41 are Rab-specific subunits located at the tail and head of HOPS, respectively.
source: HOPS has four central subunits Vps11, Vps18, Vps16, and Vps33 (Rieder and Emr, 1997), which are flanked by Vps39 and Vps41 as Rab-specific subunits at its tail and head, respectively (Brett et al., 2008; Bröcker et al., 2012; Ostrowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brett et al., 2008; Bröcker et al., 2012; Ostrowicz et al., 2010

claim: In its compact form, HOPS is about 30 nm in length and 10 nm in width.
source: In its compact form, HOPS is about 30 nm in length and 10 nm in width (Bröcker et al., 2012), whereas the more open conformation of a second study suggests an even longer particle (Chou et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bröcker et al., 2012

claim: Ypt7 has an N-terminal GTPase domain, followed by a hypervariable domain (HVD), and a C-terminal prenyl group.
source: Like all Rabs, Ypt7 has an N-terminal GTPase domain, followed by a hypervariable domain (HVD), and a C-terminal prenyl group (Goody et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Goody et al., 2017

claim: The HVD varies in length between different Rab proteins and is critical for functionality.
source: The HVD varies in length between different Rab proteins and is critical for functionality (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2014

claim: Ypt7 recruitment to membranes required the prenyl anchor and GTP to prevent GDI-mediated extraction.
source: To test membrane binding, we incubated mNeon-pYpt7:GDI with liposomes by destabilizing the interaction with GDI, and observed that Ypt7 recruitment required the prenyl anchor and GTP to prevent GDI-mediated extraction (Figure 3D).
evidence: Demonstrated by membrane binding assays shown in Figure 3D

claim: HOPS triggered liposome clustering in a pYpt7 and concentration-dependent manner.
source: In agreement with previous work (Lürick et al., 2017; Orr et al., 2015), HOPS triggered liposome clustering in a pYpt7 and concentration-dependent manner (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Demonstrated by liposome clustering assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, consistent with previous studies

claim: Active mNeon-pYpt7 was located 4.5 ± 0.3 nm above the lipid monolayer surface in the absence of effector proteins.
source: pYpt7 was located surprisingly distal from the membrane in the absence of effector proteins with the mNeon fluorophore being located 4.5 ± 0.3 nm above the lipid monolayer surface.
evidence: Calculated from fluorescence lifetime measurements using GIET calibration

claim: The site of mNeon fusion on Ypt7 is only approximately 1 nm away from the N-terminus of the HVD.
source: The site of mNeon fusion on Ypt7 is only ~1 nm away from the N-terminus of the HVD (Wiegandt et al., 2015) and therefore this observation suggests a rather extended conformation of the HVD.
evidence: Based on structural information from Wiegandt et al., 2015

claim: Upon interaction with Mon1-Ccz1, the distance of mNeon-pYpt7 decreased by 0.7 nm.
source: Upon interaction with Mon1-Ccz1 the distance of mNeon-pYpt7 decreased by 0.7 nm, while a further increase in the axial distance by 0.7 nm was observed in the presence of HOPS (Figure 3F).
evidence: Measured by GIET as shown in Figure 3F

claim: In the presence of HOPS, the axial distance of mNeon-pYpt7 increased by 0.7 nm compared to the Mon1-Ccz1 condition.
source: Upon interaction with Mon1-Ccz1 the distance of mNeon-pYpt7 decreased by 0.7 nm, while a further increase in the axial distance by 0.7 nm was observed in the presence of HOPS (Figure 3F).
evidence: Measured by GIET as shown in Figure 3F

claim: The HOPS complex binds Ypt7-GTP via its subunits Vps39 and Vps41.
source: The HOPS complex binds Ypt7-GTP via its subunits Vps39 and Vps41 (Brett et al., 2008; Ostrowicz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brett et al., 2008; Ostrowicz et al., 2010

claim: Vps39 and Vps41 have been mapped to opposite ends of the HOPS complex.
source: Since these subunits have been mapped to opposite ends of the HOPS complex (Bröcker et al., 2012), HOPS may be oriented differently on membranes, depending whether it binds Ypt7 via one or both sites.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bröcker et al., 2012

claim: HOPS clusters upon binding to diffusive membrane-anchored pYpt7-GTP.
source: Significantly heterogeneous intensity distribution of yEGFP-tagged HOPS was observed on lipid bilayers but not on lipid monolayers on graphene (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1). These results suggest that HOPS clusters upon binding to diffusive membrane-anchored pYpt7-GTP, in line with the above-mentioned clustering and loss in mobility of mNeon-pYpt7-GTP upon binding to untagged HOPS (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Inferred from heterogeneous distribution on bilayers but not monolayers, shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The two subunits at the putative HOPS tail, Vps39 (9.5 nm) and Vps11 (8.5 nm), were found to be much closer to the membrane than those of the head (Vps16 at 12.0 nm, Vps18 at 11.4 nm, and Vps33 at 11.5 nm).
source: The two subunits at the putative HOPS tail, Vps39 (9.5 nm) and Vps11 (8.5 nm), were found to be much closer to the membrane than those of the previously annotated head (Vps16 at 12.0 nm, Vps18 at 11.4 nm, and Vps33 at 11.5 nm) (Figure 4G).
evidence: Measured by GIET for different yEGFP-tagged HOPS subunits as shown in Figure 4G

claim: Membrane anchoring of HOPS with membrane-anchored Ypt7-GTP occurs exclusively via interaction of Vps39.
source: These results suggest membrane anchoring of HOPS with membrane-anchored Ypt7-GTP occurs exclusively via interaction of Vps39, in line with its higher affinity as compared to Vps41 (Lürick et al., 2017; Plemel et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from axial distance measurements and supported by citations to Lürick et al., 2017; Plemel et al., 2011

claim: The approximately 8 nm distance of the head subunits Vps33 and Vps16 from Ypt7-GTP is significantly lower than the approximately 20 nm head-to-tail distance observed in the EM structure of isolated HOPS.
source: The ~8 nm distance of the head subunits Vps33 and Vps16 from Ypt7-GTP found by GIET analyses, however, is significantly lower than the ~20 nm head-to-tail distance (between Vps33/16 and Vps39) observed in the EM structure of isolated HOPS (Bröcker et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison of GIET measurements with EM structure from Bröcker et al., 2012

claim: The HOPS complex adopts a more compact structure upon docking to membrane-anchored Ypt7-GTP.
source: These findings suggest that the HOPS complex adopts a more compact structure upon docking to membrane-anchored Ypt7-GTP.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of measured distances with EM structure

claim: The 97.7% transparency of graphene monolayer for visible light allows single-molecule imaging on graphene by TIRF microscopy with minimum loss of photons.
source: The 97.7% transparency of graphene monolayer for visible light (Nair et al., 2008) allows single-molecule imaging on graphene by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy with minimum loss of photons.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nair et al., 2008

claim: Analysis of approximately 100 single step bleaching fluorescence traces yielded IG/I0 of 0.76 ± 0.20 for HOPS Vps33 and 0.53 ± 0.14 for HOPS Vps11.
source: Analysis of ~100 single step bleaching fluorescence traces yielded IG/I0 of 0.76 ± 0.20 for HOPS Vps33 and 0.53 ± 0.14 for HOPS Vps11 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: Measured from single-molecule photobleaching analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: Single-molecule fluorescence of the HOPS complex bound to graphene-supported lipid monolayers showed pronounced fluctuations, which was not observed on glass.
source: Strikingly, single-molecule fluorescence of the HOPS complex bound to graphene-supported lipid monolayers showed pronounced fluctuations, which was not observed on glass (Figure 5A,B, Video 3).
evidence: Observed in single-molecule imaging shown in Figure 5A,B and Video 3

claim: HMM analysis identified three distinct states with 'low' (L), 'medium' (M), and 'high' (H) intensity for both HOPS variants on graphene.
source: Analysis by Hidden Markov Modeling (HMM) (McKinney et al., 2006) identified three distinct states with 'low' (L), 'medium' (M), and 'high' (H) intensity, respectively, for both HOPS variants on graphene.
evidence: Determined by HMM analysis of single-molecule intensity traces

claim: The similar changes of mean axial distance from L to M state (approximately 2 nm) in both HOPS Vps33-yEGFP and HOPS Vps11-yEGFP suggest a largely concerted axial movement of the entire HOPS complex.
source: The similar changes of mean axial distance from L to M state (~2 nm) in both HOPS Vps33-yEGFP and HOPS Vps11-yEGFP suggest a largely concerted axial movement of the entire HOPS complex.
evidence: Inferred from similar distance changes observed for both labeled subunits

claim: The high discrepancy of distance changes during transitions from M to H (Vps33: 4.4 nm; Vps11: 2 nm) indicate a conformational re-organization of the HOPS complex itself, thus adopting an elongated conformation.
source: By contrast, the high discrepancy of distance changes during transitions from M to H (Vps33: 4.4 nm; Vps11: 2 nm) indicate a conformational re-organization of the HOPS complex itself, thus adopting an elongated conformation (Figure 5F).
evidence: Inferred from differential distance changes between the two labeled subunits

claim: The conformational dynamic distance range on the membrane was approximately 7 nm for HOPS Vps33-yEGFP and 4 nm for HOPS Vps11-yEGFP.
source: In total, the conformational dynamic distance range on the membrane was ~7 nm for HOPS Vps33-yEGFP and 4 nm for HOPS Vps11-yEGFP, respectively.
evidence: Calculated from the range of distances observed across the three states

claim: The time-resolved smGIET experiments reveal a 2-step conformational transition of the Ypt7-anchored HOPS complex from the 'closed' state L to the 'open' state H via an intermediate state M.
source: Together, the time-resolved smGIET experiments reveal a 2-step conformational transition of the Ypt7-anchored HOPS complex from the 'closed' state L to the 'open' state H via an intermediate state M (Figure 5I).
evidence: Inferred from HMM analysis of state transitions shown in Figure 5I

claim: The axial localization precision of smGIET is 10.6% of the corresponding distance.
source: Thus, the relative single-molecule axial localization precision was 10.6% of the corresponding distance.
evidence: Calculated from error propagation analysis described in Materials and methods

claim: Given the sensitive range of GIET in 3–30 nm, the corresponding axial precision is in the range of 0.3–3 nm.
source: Given the sensitive range of GIET in 3–30 nm, the corresponding axial precision is in the range of 0.3–3 nm.
evidence: Calculated from the relative precision and the dynamic range

claim: GIET ideally fills the gap left by FRET and localization microscopy in the spatial regime of 10-20 nm.
source: Thus, the spatial regime covered by GIET ideally fills the gap left by FRET and localization microscopy.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of GIET dynamic range with limitations of FRET and localization microscopy

claim: The HVD of Ypt7 adopts a strongly extended conformation, locating Ypt7 at a 4.5 nm distance above the membrane surface.
source: We show that the HVD domain of Ypt7 adopts a strongly extended conformation, locating Ypt7 at a 4.5 nm distance above the membrane surface.
evidence: Measured by GIET and inferred from the position of the mNeon tag

claim: The extended conformation of the HVD could be explained by electrostatic repulsion of the negatively charged HVD.
source: This surprising observation could be explained by electrostatic repulsion of the negatively charged HVD.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed extended conformation

claim: Mon1-Ccz1 directly binds to the membrane.
source: Since Mon1-Ccz1 directly binds to the membrane (Cabrera et al., 2014), its Ypt7 binding site appears to be located distally to the membrane and the HVD allows unhindered access.
evidence: Supported by citation to Cabrera et al., 2014

claim: The conformationally highly dynamic HOPS complex observed may represent an intermediate state prior to lateral HOPS clustering.
source: Given the impaired diffusion in the graphene-supported lipid monolayer, however, the conformationally highly dynamic HOPS complex observed in our studies may represent an intermediate state prior to lateral HOPS clustering, which in turn could increase the efficiency of HOPS to tether incoming vesicles.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the observed dynamics

claim: GIET has negligible variation between spectrally different fluorophores.
source: Since GIET has negligible variation between spectrally different fluorophores (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), concerted conformational changes and axial movement can be potentially resolved by multicolor GIET.
evidence: Shown in simulations in Figure 2—figure supplement 2
